title: Pillar III — Node.js, APIs & Async Control Flow

sections.heading: The event loop: one thread, no waiting
paragraphs: Node runs your JavaScript on a single thread. It handles thousands of simultaneous connections anyway because I/O (disk, network, database) doesn't happen on that thread — Node hands the operation to the system, registers a callback, and moves on.

The event loop is the dispatcher: when the call stack is empty, it pulls completed callbacks from the queues and runs them. Microtasks (resolved promises) run before macrotasks (timers, I/O callbacks) — which is why `Promise.resolve().then(...)` beats `setTimeout(..., 0)`.
The corollary: CPU-heavy synchronous code is poison. While your JavaScript runs, nothing else runs — every pending request waits behind your loop.
sections.summary: Node juggles many requests on one thread, so any slow number-crunching code freezes everything until it finishes — keep CPU work off the loop.

variants.question: An Express server handles one route that synchronously computes a huge report for 3 seconds. During those 3 seconds, what happens to other incoming requests?
options: They queue and wait, since the busy JS thread dispatches nothing
Node automatically rejects every one of them with a 503 error response
They are all handled just fine because Express keeps each request isolated
Node quietly spawns one thread per request, so they all proceed normally
variants.rationale: One thread runs all JavaScript. A 3-second synchronous computation blocks the event loop, so every other request — even trivial health checks — waits the full 3 seconds. Fixes: chunk the work, move it to a worker thread, or push it to a job queue.
optionExplanations: Correct — 'blocking the event loop' means exactly this: everything stalls behind synchronous work.
Node sends nothing automatically; connections just sit in the queue, timing out at the client's discretion.
Express routes share the same single thread; isolation is logical, not computational.
That's the Java/traditional model. Node's whole design is one JS thread plus non-blocking I/O — no thread per request.
variants.interviewTip: 'How does Node handle concurrency with one thread?' — answer with the split: I/O concurrency comes free from the event loop; CPU concurrency requires worker threads or separate processes.

variants.question: Inside a request handler you write `Promise.resolve().then(() => log('A')); setTimeout(() => log('B'), 0); log('C');`. In what order do A, B, and C print?
options: A, B, C — any queued callback always runs before the synchronous code does
C, A, B — synchronous first, then the promise microtask, then the timer
C, B, A — the timer was registered before the promise resolved, so B wins the tie
A, C, B — the resolved promise's callback is hoisted ahead of the synchronous log
variants.rationale: `log('C')` is synchronous and runs immediately while the stack is unwinding. When the stack empties, the event loop drains the microtask queue (the resolved promise's `.then`) before any macrotask, so A prints next. `setTimeout` schedules a macrotask, which runs last — giving C, A, B.
optionExplanations: Synchronous code on the current stack always runs before any queued callback — the queues are only serviced once the stack is empty.
Correct — synchronous first (C), then microtasks (A), then macrotasks (B). Microtasks always beat timers.
Registration order across queue types is irrelevant: microtasks are drained fully before the loop touches the timer queue, so A precedes B regardless.
Nothing is 'hoisted' — the `.then` callback cannot run until the current synchronous stack (including `log('C')`) completes.
variants.interviewTip: The reliable ordering rule to state: 'current synchronous stack → drain all microtasks → one macrotask → repeat.' `Promise` callbacks are microtasks; `setTimeout`/`setImmediate`/I/O are macrotasks.

variants.question: Under a burst of logins, your `/healthz` endpoint starts timing out even though it only returns `{ ok: true }`. Profiling shows each login calls `bcrypt.hashSync` (~80ms of pure CPU). Why is the health check affected, and what's the right fix?
options: The health route shares the login route's DB connection pool; enlarging that pool restores its response times entirely
Each 80ms hash monopolizes the JS thread and queued logins stack up, so the health callback waits; use async `bcrypt.hash`
HTTP keep-alive is pinning the health check's socket behind the login sockets; disabling keep-alive on the server fixes it
Node schedules routes by their registration order, so simply registering `/healthz` before the login route restores it fully
variants.rationale: 80ms of synchronous CPU doesn't sound like much, but under a login burst those blocks queue back-to-back on the single JS thread, and every other callback — including a trivial health check — waits behind the entire backlog. The async `bcrypt.hash` runs the hashing off the JS thread (libuv threadpool), keeping the loop free to dispatch other work; worker threads are the general answer for CPU-bound code.
optionExplanations: There is no connection pool between routes — the contention is on the JS thread itself, and no pool setting frees it.
Correct — the symptom of event-loop blocking is unrelated endpoints getting slow; the fix is moving CPU work off the JS thread, not tuning the fast route.
Keep-alive reuses sockets; it doesn't serialize unrelated requests. The stall happens after the request arrives, in the blocked loop.
Route registration order affects matching, not scheduling — a registered-first route still can't run while the thread is executing someone else's hash.
variants.interviewTip: Latency spikes on a trivially cheap endpoint are the textbook symptom of event-loop blocking. Diagnosing from the victim endpoint rather than the guilty one is exactly the reasoning interviewers want to hear.

variants.question: A handler runs: `setTimeout(() => log('T'), 0); (async () => { log('S'); await null; log('W'); })(); log('E');`. What prints, in order?
options: S, W, E, T — the async function runs fully to completion before control returns to its caller
E, S, W, T — async function bodies are wholly deferred to the microtask queue right from the start
S, E, W, T — sync prefix runs, `E` ends the stack, the continuation is a microtask, timer last
S, E, T, W — the timer was queued before the `await` ran, so it fires before the continuation does
variants.rationale: Calling an async function executes its body synchronously up to the first `await` — so S prints during the call. `await null` suspends the function and control returns to the caller, which prints E. When the stack empties, the continuation (W) runs from the microtask queue before the loop services the timer queue, so T is last: S, E, W, T.
optionExplanations: An async function yields at its first `await`; it does not run to completion before returning — that's the whole point of the suspension.
The body is not deferred: everything before the first `await` executes synchronously during the call, so S beats E.
Correct — synchronous prefix (S), rest of the stack (E), microtask continuation (W), then the macrotask timer (T).
Queue registration time doesn't matter across queue types: microtasks are drained completely before any timer runs, so W always precedes T.
variants.interviewTip: The nuance interviewers probe: `await` splits an async function into a synchronous prefix and a microtask continuation. Say 'runs synchronously until the first await' and you've disarmed the whole question family.

sections.heading: Promises and async/await
paragraphs: A promise is a placeholder for a value that isn't ready: pending, then either fulfilled or rejected. `async/await` is syntax over promises — `await` pauses that async function (not the thread!) until the promise settles.

The classic performance mistake is sequential awaiting of independent work: `const a = await getA(); const b = await getB();` takes the sum of both latencies. Independent operations should start together: `const [a, b] = await Promise.all([getA(), getB()]);` — now you pay only the slower one.

Know the combinators: `Promise.all` fails fast on the first rejection; `Promise.allSettled` waits for every result, success or failure; `Promise.race` settles with whichever finishes first; `Promise.any` returns the first fulfilment and ignores rejections until all fail. Pick by what you need: all-or-nothing, every-outcome, first-done, or first-success.
sections.summary: When tasks don't depend on each other, start them together with `Promise.all` so you wait once, not one after another — and match the combinator to whether you need all results, every outcome, or just the first.

variants.question: getUser() takes ~200ms and getOrders() takes ~300ms; they don't depend on each other. `await getUser(); await getOrders();` takes ~500ms total. What change gets it to ~300ms?
options: Use `process.nextTick` to prioritize the two calls in the loop
Wrap both of the awaits together inside one try/catch block
Start both promises first, then await: `Promise.all([...])`
Convert both async functions to blocking synchronous versions
variants.rationale: Sequential awaits serialize independent I/O. Promise.all starts both immediately and resolves when the slowest settles — total time becomes max(200, 300) ≈ 300ms instead of the 500ms sum.
optionExplanations: process.nextTick reorders microtask timing by microseconds; it cannot overlap two network calls.
try/catch changes error handling, not scheduling — still 500ms.
Correct — concurrent start, single await, pay only the slowest.
Synchronous I/O would block the entire event loop for 500ms — dramatically worse for every other request.
variants.interviewTip: Spotting 'sequential awaits on independent operations' in a code-review interview is a rehearsed scenario at many companies. Scan for it explicitly.

variants.question: You fire five independent inventory lookups with `const results = await Promise.all(calls);`. One of the five services is down and its promise rejects. What does `results` end up being, and what's the fix if you need every store's status regardless?
options: `Promise.all` retries the failed call automatically, so `results` eventually fills in fully
`results` becomes an array of pending promises you must then await individually afterward
`results` holds the four successes with `undefined` sitting in the failed slot; no change needed
The whole `await` rejects and `results` is never assigned — swap to `Promise.allSettled`
variants.rationale: `Promise.all` fails fast: the first rejection rejects the aggregate immediately, so the `await` throws and `results` is never bound — the four successes are discarded. When you need every result whether it succeeded or failed, `Promise.allSettled` resolves to an array of `{status, value|reason}` objects, one per input.
optionExplanations: `Promise.all` has no retry behavior; it only aggregates settlement — you'd build retries yourself.
`Promise.all` returns a single promise resolving to an array of values, not an array of promises.
`Promise.all` does not substitute `undefined` for failures; a single rejection discards the entire aggregate result.
Correct — `all` rejects on first failure; `allSettled` waits for all and reports each outcome individually.
variants.interviewTip: Know the combinator table cold: `all` (fail-fast, all-or-nothing), `allSettled` (never rejects, per-item outcomes), `race` (first to settle wins), `any` (first to fulfill, ignores rejections until all fail).

variants.question: `for (const id of skus) { prices.push(await fetchPrice(id)); }` over 10 independent SKUs at ~120ms each takes ~1.2s. Which rewrite brings it to ~120ms, and why?
options: `await Promise.all(skus.map((id) => fetchPrice(id)))` — `map` fires all ten at once, so one await pays the slowest
Replace `for...of` with `skus.forEach(async (id) => ...)` — the body then runs in parallel and `prices` fills right after
Move each loop iteration into `process.nextTick` so that the pending fetches interleave between the loop's turns
Switch to `for await (const id of skus)` — `for await` makes any loop's iterations run concurrently and automatically
variants.rationale: The `await` inside the loop body means iteration N+1 can't even start its request until N's response arrives — ten sequential 120ms round-trips. Mapping to an array of promises starts all ten requests in the same tick; the one `await Promise.all` then resolves when the slowest settles, so total time collapses to roughly max instead of sum.
optionExplanations: Correct — start-all-then-await-once is the pattern; the requests overlap in flight and you pay ~max(latencies) instead of their sum.
`forEach` ignores the promises its async callback returns — the loop 'finishes' instantly while every fetch is still pending, and `prices` is empty (or partially filled) when you read it.
`process.nextTick` shuffles microtask timing; the loop still awaits each response before issuing the next request, so it stays ~1.2s.
`for await` changes how an async iterable is consumed; with the fetch call still inside the body, each iteration still awaits before the next one starts.
variants.interviewTip: 'await in a loop' is the code-review flag interviewers plant deliberately. The follow-up they want: when the list is large, cap concurrency (batching or a limiter like `p-limit`) rather than firing thousands of requests at once.

variants.question: You migrate a batch notifier from `Promise.all` to `Promise.allSettled` and keep the surrounding `try/catch` to log failures. Sends fail all week, but the `catch` block never fires and nothing is logged. What's happening?
options: `allSettled` permanently swallows the errors, so once it is in place every single failure becomes unobservable
The `try/catch` here is simply scoped wrong — moving it inside each individual promise callback restores the logging
The promise `allSettled` returns never rejects — failures arrive as `{status:'rejected'}` entries you inspect
`allSettled` quietly retries each of the failed promises until they eventually succeed, so no failures remain to log
variants.rationale: `Promise.allSettled` fulfills unconditionally with one descriptor per input: `{status: 'fulfilled', value}` or `{status: 'rejected', reason}`. Since the aggregate never rejects, the `await` never throws, and a `try/catch` around it is dead code for per-item failures. Error handling must move from exception flow to data flow: iterate the results and act on the rejected entries.
optionExplanations: Nothing is swallowed — every failure is right there in the result array as a `reason`; it's just delivered as data, not as a thrown exception.
Relocating the `try/catch` misses the point: the design of `allSettled` is that failures are reported in the fulfillment value, not thrown anywhere.
Correct — switching combinators changes the error-delivery channel from throw to data; code that only listens for throws goes silently blind.
No combinator retries anything; `allSettled` simply waits for every input to settle once and reports what happened.
variants.interviewTip: A sharp follow-up you can preempt: 'When would allSettled hide bugs?' — when callers forget that error handling moved into the result array. Pair any `allSettled` with an explicit pass over the `rejected` entries.

sections.heading: Designing REST APIs
paragraphs: REST URLs name resources with nouns; HTTP methods supply the verbs. `GET /users/42/orders` reads orders for user 42. `POST /orders` creates. Verbs in URLs (`/getUser`, `/createOrder`) are the RPC habit REST replaces.

Respond with codes that match what happened: `201 Created` (with a `Location` header) for creation, `204 No Content` for a successful delete, `400` for malformed input, `422` for well-formed input that fails validation, `404` for a missing resource.

Version your API (`/v1/...`) from day one, and never break the contract of a shipped version — clients you don't control are relying on the shape of your responses. Adding fields is safe; renaming or removing them, or tightening validation, breaks callers silently, so those changes belong in a new version.
sections.summary: Name things (nouns) in the URL, let the HTTP method be the action, send back the status code that fits what happened, and version so you never break shipped clients.

variants.question: Which endpoint design best follows REST conventions for 'cancel order 42'?
options: `POST /orders/42/cancel` (or `PATCH /orders/42` for status)
`DELETE /orders/cancel/42`, removing the cancelled order row
`PUT /cancel` carrying the order id down in the request body
`GET /cancelOrder?id=42`, passing the id as a query string
variants.rationale: Cancellation is a state transition on order 42, not a read and usually not a removal — the order record persists as 'cancelled'. Modeling it as a sub-action POST or a PATCH of the status field keeps the resource-oriented grammar while expressing a domain action.
optionExplanations: Correct — a state transition modeled on the resource. Both forms are accepted; be ready to defend either.
DELETE says the resource ceases to exist, but a cancelled order must remain queryable — plus the URL structure is scrambled.
PUT means replace the resource at this URL; '/cancel' isn't a resource, and hiding the id in the body breaks addressability.
A GET with side effects is the cardinal REST sin — prefetchers and proxies re-issue GETs freely and would cancel orders on their own.
variants.interviewTip: 'How do you model actions that aren't CRUD?' is a designed-in follow-up. The phrase to offer: 'model the state transition, not the verb' — then mention both the sub-resource POST and the PATCH approach.

variants.question: A client submits the same `POST /payments` twice because the network dropped the first response. Which HTTP-method property is at stake, and which status code correctly signals a duplicate creation attempt on a resource that already exists?
options: `GET` is idempotent, so the fix is simply to change this endpoint over to `GET /payments`
`POST` isn't idempotent; guard it with an idempotency key and return `409` on the duplicate
`POST` is idempotent, so any second identical `POST` is always safe and just returns a plain `200`
The correct response to any duplicate is `400 Bad Request`, since the client sent the request twice
variants.rationale: `POST` is neither safe nor idempotent — repeating it can create duplicate resources. The standard defense is an idempotency key the server records so a retry maps to the original operation, returning `409 Conflict` when the key collides with a different in-flight/completed create (or replaying the original `201`). This is exactly why `PUT` (idempotent) is preferred when the client controls the identifier.
optionExplanations: `GET` must be safe — it cannot create a payment at all; switching the verb loses the write semantics entirely.
Correct — `POST` isn't idempotent; idempotency keys plus `409`/replayed-`201` make retries safe without double-charging.
`POST` is explicitly non-idempotent in the HTTP spec; assuming otherwise is what causes duplicate charges.
`400` means malformed syntax; a well-formed duplicate is a conflict (`409`) or a replayed success, not a bad request.
variants.interviewTip: Memorize method properties: `GET`/`HEAD` safe + idempotent; `PUT`/`DELETE` idempotent (not safe); `POST`/`PATCH` neither. 'How do you make `POST` retry-safe?' → idempotency keys.

variants.question: Your API needs 'deactivate account 7' — the account must remain readable afterward for audit and possible reactivation. Which design best fits REST conventions?
options: `DELETE /accounts/7` — deactivation is a removal, and clients can always recreate the account afterward
`GET /accounts/deactivate/7` — reads are cache-friendly here and this URL is nicely self-describing
`PUT /deactivate` with the payload `{ "accountId": 7 }` carried in the request body instead
`POST /accounts/7/deactivation` (or `PATCH /accounts/7` setting `status:"inactive"`) — a transition
variants.rationale: Deactivation changes an account's state without removing it — the record must stay addressable for audit, support, and reactivation. That rules out `DELETE` (semantic removal) and anything with side effects on `GET`. A sub-action `POST` or a `PATCH` of the status field expresses the domain transition while keeping resource-oriented URLs.
optionExplanations: `DELETE` communicates that the resource is gone; clients and caches may treat `/accounts/7` as nonexistent afterward, breaking the audit and reactivation requirements.
A `GET` that mutates state violates safety — crawlers, prefetchers, and monitoring probes would deactivate accounts just by touching the URL.
`PUT` means 'replace the resource at this URL' — `/deactivate` names no resource, and burying the id in the body destroys addressability and idempotent-replacement semantics.
Correct — model the state transition on the resource; both the sub-action `POST` and the status `PATCH` are defensible, and you should be able to argue either.
variants.interviewTip: When an action must leave the resource queryable afterward, that single requirement eliminates `DELETE` for you — lead with it. 'Soft-delete vs hard-delete' is the natural follow-up, so have a one-liner ready on status flags vs row removal.

variants.question: An API gateway automatically re-sends any request that times out. Which endpoint below can it safely re-send without server-side deduplication, and what property makes that true?
options: `PUT /shipments/3f9a` with the full body — `PUT` is idempotent, so replaying a full replacement converges
`POST /shipments` — creation endpoints are always replay-safe here because the server assigns each of the ids
`PATCH /shipments/3f9a` with `{ "op":"increment", "retries":1 }` — a `PATCH` is idempotent by its definition
None — no HTTP method whatsoever may ever be safely retried, so the gateway's feature must be disabled
variants.rationale: Idempotency means N identical requests leave the server in the same state as one. A `PUT` of the full representation to a client-chosen URL has exactly that property — replaying it just rewrites the same bytes. A bare `POST` create mints a new resource per replay, and an increment-style `PATCH` compounds on every retry: both need deduplication (idempotency keys) before blind retries are safe.
optionExplanations: Correct — full-replacement `PUT` at a known URL is the canonical retry-safe write; this is precisely why client-generated ids plus `PUT` are favored in retry-heavy systems.
Server-assigned ids are exactly the problem: each replayed `POST` looks like a fresh create, so the gateway would mint duplicate shipments.
`PATCH` carries no idempotency guarantee — it depends entirely on the patch semantics, and an increment operation is the textbook non-idempotent counterexample.
Idempotent methods exist specifically so infrastructure can retry them; forbidding all retries throws away the guarantee the spec provides.
variants.interviewTip: When asked about retry-safe API design, volunteer the design move — 'let the client generate the id and use `PUT`' — rather than just reciting the method table. It shows you can build idempotency, not just define it.

sections.heading: Middleware and the request pipeline
paragraphs: In Express-style frameworks, a request flows through a chain of middleware functions: `(req, res, next)`. Each can inspect or modify the request, end the response, or call `next()` to pass control down the chain. Order of registration is order of execution.

This is where cross-cutting concerns live: body parsing, logging, rate limiting, authentication, authorization. An auth middleware that finds no valid token responds 401 and simply never calls next() — short-circuiting the pipeline.

Error handling gets its own shape: a four-argument middleware `(err, req, res, next)` registered last. Async route errors must reach it — in Express 4 that means catching and calling `next(err)` (Express 5 forwards rejected promises automatically).
sections.summary: Requests pass through your middleware in the order you register them, so put things like auth and body parsing before the routes they support — and give error handling its own four-argument handler at the end.

variants.question: A developer registers routes first and the authentication middleware after them: `app.use('/api', routes); app.use(authMiddleware);`. What's the consequence?
options: Nothing at all — middleware registration order doesn't matter in Express
Express detects the ordering mistake and quietly reorders them at startup
Routes run before auth executes, so each `/api` route is unauthenticated
The auth middleware ends up running twice on every single request instead here
variants.rationale: Middleware executes in registration order. A request matching /api hits the route handler, which sends a response — the chain never reaches authMiddleware. Order-dependent security is why auth registration belongs above the routes it protects.
optionExplanations: Order is the single most important property of a middleware pipeline.
Express has no dependency analysis; registration order is the contract, and it trusts you.
Correct — and it fails open: everything works in testing, except nothing is protected.
It runs zero times for matched routes, not twice — the response ends the chain first.
variants.interviewTip: Security bugs that 'fail open' (system works, protection silently absent) make strong interview stories. This ordering bug is a perfect concrete example to have in your pocket.

variants.question: An async route handler in Express 4 throws inside a rejected `await`, but the developer forgot to `catch` it. The four-argument error middleware is registered correctly at the end. Why does the client still hang instead of getting a clean 500?
options: Registering the error handler last is itself the bug here; it has to be registered first instead
Throwing inside `await` crashes the whole process instantly, so no response can ever be sent back
The error middleware actually needs five arguments, not four, to catch these async errors properly
Express 4 won't forward a rejected promise to the error handler, so `next(err)` is never called
variants.rationale: Express 4 only routes errors to the `(err, req, res, next)` handler when you synchronously throw or explicitly call `next(err)`. An unhandled promise rejection in an async handler is invisible to that mechanism — nothing calls `next(err)`, no response is written, and the socket stays open until it times out. The fix is a try/catch that calls `next(err)` (or an async wrapper); Express 5 forwards rejections automatically.
optionExplanations: Error handlers are meant to be registered last, after the routes whose errors they catch — that ordering is correct here.
An unhandled rejection may log a warning but does not synchronously crash the process; the request simply never gets a response.
Four arguments is exactly what marks a middleware as an error handler; five would not be recognized as one.
Correct — Express 4 needs `next(err)`; a bare async rejection bypasses the error pipeline and leaves the request hanging.
variants.interviewTip: 'How do async errors reach Express error middleware?' → Express 4: you must `catch` and `next(err)` (or use `express-async-errors`/a wrapper); Express 5: rejected promises are forwarded for you.

variants.question: A teammate registers routes before the parsers: `app.use('/api', apiRoutes); app.use(express.json());`. POSTs to `/api` now misbehave. What do the route handlers actually observe, and why?
options: Express buffers each request until every registered middleware has run, so the handlers still see parsed bodies
`req.body` is `undefined` in every handler — the router matches first, so requests arrive before parsing
Express throws an error at startup here because the parsers must always be registered ahead of any of the routers
Handlers instead receive the raw request body as a plain string and must call `JSON.parse` on it themselves
variants.rationale: Registration order is execution order. A POST to `/api` matches the router immediately, the handler runs, and `express.json()` — sitting later in the chain — never gets a chance to read and parse the stream. The handler sees `req.body === undefined`, and the failure is quiet: no error, just missing data, often surfacing as a confusing `TypeError` deep in business logic.
optionExplanations: There is no buffering-until-registration-complete phase; the chain runs top-down per request and stops progressing once a handler responds.
Correct — parsers only populate `req.body` for middleware and handlers positioned after them; upstream handlers see nothing.
Express performs no startup validation of middleware order — it trusts registration order completely, which is exactly why this class of bug ships.
Without a body-parsing middleware having run, `req.body` isn't a raw string — it's simply `undefined`; the unread stream is still sitting on the request.
variants.interviewTip: Same root cause as the auth-after-routes bug — order is the contract — but this variant fails with missing data instead of missing security. Naming both consequences of one principle is a strong interview move.

variants.question: Errors forwarded with `next(err)` skip your custom handler and fall through to Express's default HTML error page. The handler is registered last, after all routes: `app.use((err, req, res) => { res.status(500).json({ error: 'oops' }); });`. Why is it never invoked?
options: Express identifies error middleware purely by arity, so a three-parameter function counts as ordinary middleware; declare all four
`next(err)` can only ever reach the handlers that were registered before the route which actually raised the error itself here
Custom JSON error responses always require fully replacing Express's built-in default error handler through an explicit `app.set` call
The handler must first call `next()` once with no arguments at all before it ever becomes eligible to receive any of the errors
variants.rationale: Express inspects `fn.length` — the declared parameter count — to classify middleware. Exactly four parameters marks an error handler; anything else is regular middleware, which the error-dispatch path skips entirely. Parameter names are irrelevant, so `(err, req, res)` silently registers as a normal three-argument middleware and errors sail past it to the default handler.
optionExplanations: Correct — the arity check is the contract; keep the fourth parameter even if unused (convention: `(err, req, res, next)`, often with `next` untouched).
It's the reverse: `next(err)` skips remaining regular middleware and searches forward for error handlers, which is why they belong at the end.
No `app.set` incantation is involved — any correctly-declared four-argument middleware that sends a response overrides the default page.
There's no eligibility handshake; classification happens at registration time from the function signature, before any request flows.
variants.interviewTip: That Express dispatches on `fn.length` is a detail most candidates don't know — mentioning it (and its gotcha: rest parameters or dropping an unused arg silently changes arity) reads as real production experience.

sections.heading: Failing well: errors, timeouts, retries
paragraphs: Every await can reject. Unhandled rejections in a server context mean crashed requests or, worse, a crashed process. Route-level try/catch (or a wrapper) funneling into a central error handler gives you one place for logging and consistent error responses.

Never trust an external call to return promptly — attach timeouts (AbortController) so a hung upstream doesn't pin your requests forever. Retry transient failures with exponential backoff, and only retry operations that are idempotent or de-duplicated.
Separate expected failures (validation, not-found — clean 4xx responses) from unexpected ones (bugs, upstream outages — 5xx, logged loudly with a correlation id, message kept vague to the client).
sections.summary: Assume outside calls can hang or fail: set timeouts, retry gently (with backoff and jitter), and only retry when doing it twice is safe — and keep expected 4xx failures separate from logged-loudly 5xx ones.

variants.question: A payment provider call occasionally hangs for minutes. The team adds an aggressive automatic retry (3 attempts, no backoff, no idempotency key). What's the biggest risk?
options: Duplicate charges: a hung request may have succeeded already, so non-idempotent retries repeat it
The TypeScript compiler will statically flag the whole retry loop here as being unsafe at build time
Retrying an operation is essentially impossible when you are using async/await syntax here
The three retries end up consuming far too much heap memory on the client machine itself
variants.rationale: A timeout tells you the response didn't arrive — not that the operation didn't happen. Retrying a possibly-succeeded charge without an idempotency key risks charging twice. Backoff with jitter matters too: immediate uniform retries pile onto an already-degraded service.
optionExplanations: Correct — retry safety = idempotency + backoff. Both are missing here, and money makes the failure expensive.
Type checkers know nothing of retry semantics; this bug type-checks perfectly.
Retry loops with async/await are routine — a for-loop with try/catch and a delay.
Three retries hold trivial memory; the risk is on the money, not the RAM.
variants.interviewTip: The distilled principle for system-design rounds: 'timeouts bound your waiting, retries need idempotency, backoff protects the upstream.' Three clauses, huge signal.

variants.question: A service fronts a flaky third-party API. Under load, a spike of failures triggers thousands of simultaneous retries that all fire again at the exact same interval, repeatedly knocking the recovering upstream back down. Backoff is already in place. What's missing?
options: Nothing at all — synchronized retries are the correct behavior here; the upstream should simply scale up itself
Jitter: randomize each backoff delay so retries spread out instead of aligning into thundering-herd waves
The retry count is far too low here; raising it up to 10 attempts will reliably push through the whole outage
Switching over from exponential backoff to plain linear backoff will fix the retry alignment problem here
variants.rationale: Fixed exponential backoff makes every failed caller wait the same computed delay, so they all retry in lockstep — a self-inflicted thundering herd that prevents recovery. Randomized jitter decorrelates the retries across time, and a circuit breaker trips after sustained failure to stop hammering the upstream and fail fast until it's healthy again.
optionExplanations: Synchronized retry storms actively obstruct recovery; expecting the upstream to absorb a self-inflicted herd is not a real fix.
Correct — jitter decorrelates the retry timing and a circuit breaker halts retries against a downed dependency.
More attempts multiplies the load on an already-struggling service, deepening the outage rather than resolving it.
Linear backoff still fires all callers at identical (just differently spaced) instants; without randomness they stay synchronized.
variants.interviewTip: The phrase interviewers listen for is 'exponential backoff *with jitter*' — plus a circuit breaker for sustained failure. Backoff alone still lets retries synchronize into a thundering herd.

variants.question: Your checkout service calls a shipping-rates API with idempotent retries and jittered exponential backoff — yet during an upstream incident, in-flight requests pile up for minutes and the Node process exhausts its sockets. Which safeguard is missing?
options: A higher retry cap, so that the piled-up requests eventually punch their way through the whole incident
A `Promise.race` against a `setInterval` that keeps polling the upstream repeatedly over and over until it finally responds
A per-attempt timeout (`AbortController` + `signal`) — retries only act after a failure, so nothing bounds a hung attempt
Moving all of the calls into a worker thread so that the hung requests will then only block that one worker
variants.rationale: Retry logic activates on failure — but a hung socket isn't a failure yet; it's an attempt that never resolves. Without a timeout, 'slow' never converts into 'failed', so backoff and retries sit idle while open connections accumulate and starve the process. An `AbortController` deadline per attempt turns hangs into prompt errors that the (already correct) retry machinery can handle.
optionExplanations: More attempts multiplies pressure on a struggling upstream and does nothing for the attempts currently hung — the first try still never returns.
Racing a promise abandons your handler's wait but doesn't cancel the underlying request — the socket stays open, which is precisely the resource being exhausted.
Correct — timeouts bound the waiting; they're the trigger that lets retry-with-backoff engage at all. Without them the rest of the resilience stack is unreachable.
I/O waits don't occupy the JS thread anyway; the exhausted resource is sockets/file descriptors, which worker threads share with the main process.
variants.interviewTip: A subtle point worth stating: `Promise.race`-based 'timeouts' orphan the request rather than cancel it. `AbortController` actually tears down the connection — that distinction separates senior answers from rehearsed ones.

variants.question: To make payment retries safe, a developer generates a fresh UUID idempotency key inside the retry loop — a new key per attempt. Retries 'work', but duplicate charges still appear after timeouts. What's the flaw?
options: UUIDs can quietly collide under heavy load, so two different customers occasionally end up sharing one key
Idempotency keys only ever function correctly over network connections that happen to support HTTP/2
The key should instead be derived from the card number itself so that the server can match up customers
The key must stay constant across every retry of one operation; a new key per attempt defeats dedup
variants.rationale: An idempotency key identifies the logical operation, not the network attempt. The server dedupes by recording the key with the outcome; a retry bearing the same key replays the recorded result instead of re-executing. Regenerating the key per attempt severs that link — after a timeout (where the charge may have succeeded server-side), the retry arrives with an unknown key and is processed as a second, distinct payment.
optionExplanations: UUIDv4 collision probability is negligible; the duplicates here are caused deterministically by the key rotation, not by chance.
Idempotency keys are just a request header plus server-side bookkeeping — the transport protocol version is irrelevant.
Deriving keys from card data conflates the customer with the operation (and smuggles sensitive data into headers); one customer legitimately makes many payments.
Correct — generate the key once per logical operation, outside the retry loop, and reuse it on every attempt so the server can recognize the repeat.
variants.interviewTip: The one-liner that shows mastery: 'the idempotency key's scope is the operation, not the attempt.' Follow with where it's generated — once, before the retry loop — and you've answered the implementation follow-up preemptively.

sections.heading: Streams and backpressure
paragraphs: Streams process data in chunks instead of loading it all into memory. Reading a 2GB file with `fs.readFile` buffers the whole thing into RAM before you touch a byte; `fs.createReadStream` hands you chunks as they arrive, so memory stays flat regardless of file size. This is why `pipe` (or `stream.pipeline`) is the idiom for moving bytes from a file, socket, or HTTP body to a destination.

Backpressure is the flow-control mechanism that keeps a fast source from overwhelming a slow destination. When you `pipe` a readable into a writable, `write()` returns `false` once the destination's internal buffer is full; a well-behaved pipeline pauses the source until the writable emits `drain`. Skip this — for example by ignoring `write()`'s return value in a hand-rolled loop — and the buffer grows without bound until the process runs out of memory.

Use `stream.pipeline` (or `pipeline` from `node:stream/promises`) rather than raw `.pipe()`: it wires backpressure and, crucially, propagates errors and destroys every stream in the chain on failure. A bare `.pipe()` leaks the source stream if the destination errors, because it doesn't clean up for you.
sections.summary: Streams move data in chunks so memory stays flat, and backpressure pauses a fast source when the slow destination can't keep up — use `pipeline` so errors and cleanup are handled for you.

variants.question: A service reads uploaded CSVs by calling `fs.readFile` then parsing the whole string. It works in testing but the process is OOM-killed in production on large files. What's the core fix?
options: Raise the container's memory limit so the largest expected upload fits comfortably into the process heap
Stream the file with `createReadStream` and parse chunks, so memory stays flat regardless of size
Call `global.gc()` right after each parse so the buffered file string is reclaimed sooner
Wrap the `readFile` call in a `try/catch` so the out-of-memory error is caught and retried
variants.rationale: `fs.readFile` buffers the entire file into a single Buffer/string before your code runs, so peak memory scales with file size — a large upload blows the heap. Streaming with `createReadStream` delivers chunks as they arrive and lets you parse incrementally, keeping memory bounded no matter how big the input grows.
optionExplanations: Raising the limit just moves the cliff; the next larger file OOMs again because buffering is O(file size) by design.
Correct — streaming processes the file in bounded chunks, so peak memory no longer scales with input size.
You can't reclaim memory that's still referenced mid-parse, and forcing GC is a smell that hides the real O(size) buffering problem.
An OOM often kills the process outright, and even when catchable, retrying the same buffering call reproduces the same blowup.
variants.interviewTip: When a bug is 'fine in tests, dies in prod on big inputs,' say 'buffered the whole thing into memory' before anything else — streaming is the expected fix, and it signals you think about resource bounds, not just correctness.

variants.question: In a custom pipe, a developer writes `src.on('data', c => dest.write(c))` and ignores what `write()` returns. Under a fast source and slow destination, memory climbs steadily. What did they skip?
options: Backpressure: `write()` returns `false` when the buffer is full and they must pause until `drain`
They forgot to JSON-encode each chunk before writing, so the buffer stores oversized objects
They never called `dest.end()`, so Node keeps every chunk pinned in memory until the stream closes
The `data` event fires twice per chunk, so each write silently duplicates the payload in the buffer
variants.rationale: `writable.write()` returns `false` when the destination's internal buffer has passed its high-water mark, signaling the producer to stop. Ignoring that return value means the source keeps pushing chunks into a buffer the destination can't drain fast enough, so the queued data grows without bound. The fix is to pause the source on `false` and resume on the writable's `drain` event — which is exactly what `pipe`/`pipeline` do automatically.
optionExplanations: Correct — the ignored `write()` return value is the backpressure signal; without pausing on `false`, the buffer grows unbounded.
Encoding format doesn't cause the growth; an unbounded write queue does, regardless of what the chunks contain.
Missing `end()` leaves the stream open but doesn't itself cause memory to climb under load — the unheeded backpressure does.
The `data` event fires once per chunk; there's no duplication, just a producer outrunning the consumer.
variants.interviewTip: Say the mechanism precisely: '`write()` returns false at the high-water mark; pause the readable and resume on drain.' Then add that `pipe`/`pipeline` handle this for you — reaching for them is the senior instinct.

variants.question: You replace `readable.pipe(writable)` with `stream.pipeline(readable, transform, writable, cb)`. Beyond readability, what concrete robustness problem does `pipeline` solve that bare `.pipe()` does not?
options: It compresses each chunk in transit automatically, cutting the bytes the destination must buffer
It disables backpressure so the transform stage can run at full speed without waiting on drain
It propagates errors across the chain and destroys every stream, preventing leaks on failure
It retries the whole pipeline from the start whenever any one stage emits an `error` event
variants.rationale: A bare `.pipe()` forwards data but does not forward errors: if the destination errors, the source is not destroyed and leaks (open file descriptors, sockets). `stream.pipeline` centralizes error handling — one callback (or a rejected promise with the promises variant) receives the first error, and it destroys every stream in the chain, so nothing is left dangling.
optionExplanations: `pipeline` does no compression; you'd insert a `zlib` transform yourself if you wanted that.
`pipeline` preserves backpressure just like `pipe` — it doesn't disable flow control, which would reintroduce the memory blowup.
Correct — `pipeline` propagates the first error to its callback and destroys the whole chain, closing the leaks `.pipe()` leaves open.
`pipeline` reports the error and tears down; it does not automatically retry — retry logic is yours to add around it.
variants.interviewTip: 'Why prefer `pipeline` over `.pipe()`?' has a crisp answer: error propagation and guaranteed cleanup. Bare `.pipe()` leaking the source on a destination error is a real production footgun worth naming.

variants.question: An HTTP handler pipes a huge database result to the response, but you also want to gzip it on the way out. Where does the compression belong, and what stream type is it?
options: Buffer the full result, gzip the buffer with `zlib.gzipSync`, then send it as one response body
A Transform stream (`zlib.createGzip`) placed between source and response inside the pipeline
A Writable stream at the very end that gzips only after every chunk has been fully collected
A Readable stream ahead of the query that pre-compresses rows before the database returns them
variants.rationale: Compression is a chunk-in, chunk-out operation, which is exactly a Transform stream. `zlib.createGzip()` returns one, and you place it mid-pipeline — `pipeline(dbStream, gzip, res)` — so each chunk is compressed as it flows, preserving the streaming and backpressure benefits end to end. Buffering to gzip the whole thing reintroduces the memory problem streaming was meant to avoid.
optionExplanations: Buffering the full result to gzip it defeats streaming: peak memory scales with the response size again, the exact problem you're avoiding.
Correct — gzip is a Transform (chunk-in, chunk-out); `zlib.createGzip()` sits between source and response and compresses as data flows.
A terminal Writable that waits for all chunks is just buffering in disguise; it can't emit compressed output incrementally.
You can't compress rows before the database has produced them, and a source Readable is the wrong place for a mid-stream transform.
variants.interviewTip: Map the three stream roles fast: Readable = source, Writable = sink, Transform = both (compression, encryption, parsing). Naming `createGzip` as a Transform in a pipeline shows you compose streams rather than buffer.

sections.heading: CommonJS vs ES modules
paragraphs: Node grew up on CommonJS: `require()` loads a module synchronously and returns its `module.exports` object, resolved at the moment the call runs. ES modules (ESM) use `import`/`export`, are resolved and linked before any code executes, and their bindings are live — an imported name reflects later changes to the exporter's variable, whereas a CommonJS import is a snapshot of the value at require time.

How a `.js` file is interpreted depends on the nearest `package.json`: `"type": "module"` makes `.js` files ESM, its absence (or `"type": "commonjs"`) makes them CommonJS. You can always be explicit with the `.mjs` (ESM) and `.cjs` (CommonJS) extensions. ESM is async under the hood, which unlocks top-level `await` — you can `await` at module scope without wrapping it in an async function, something CommonJS cannot do.

Interop has sharp edges. ESM can `import` a CommonJS module (its `module.exports` becomes the default export), but CommonJS cannot `require()` a true ESM module synchronously — historically you needed dynamic `import()`, which returns a promise. Globals differ too: `__dirname` and `__filename` don't exist in ESM, where you reconstruct them from `import.meta.url`.
sections.summary: CommonJS `require` is synchronous and snapshots values; ESM `import`/`export` links up front with live bindings and top-level await — and how a `.js` file is read depends on the nearest `package.json` "type".

variants.question: You add `"type": "module"` to package.json and an existing `.js` file that uses `__dirname` immediately throws `__dirname is not defined`. Why?
options: The file must be renamed to `.mjs` before Node will ever let it reference any path globals
`__dirname` is a CommonJS-only global; ESM has no such variable and derives paths from `import.meta.url`
Node caches `__dirname` once per process, and switching module type clears that cache until the next restart
The variable exists but is now read-only in strict mode, so touching it throws a reference error
variants.rationale: `__dirname` and `__filename` are injected by the CommonJS module wrapper — they simply don't exist in ES modules. Setting `"type": "module"` reinterprets your `.js` file as ESM, so those globals vanish. The ESM way to get the current directory is to derive it from `import.meta.url`, e.g. `path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url))`.
optionExplanations: Renaming to `.mjs` also makes it ESM, which removes `__dirname` too — the extension isn't the fix; reconstructing the path is.
Correct — `__dirname` belongs to the CommonJS wrapper; ESM omits it, so you rebuild it from `import.meta.url`.
There's no per-process `__dirname` cache; the variable is provided by the module system, and ESM doesn't provide it.
It's not a strict-mode read-only issue — the identifier is genuinely undefined in ESM scope.
variants.interviewTip: Keep the ESM path snippet ready: `import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url'; const __dirname = path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));`. Knowing why the globals vanish (they were wrapper injections) reads as real migration experience.

variants.question: A CommonJS module does `const cfg = require('./config'); console.log(cfg.ready);` at load time, but `config.js` sets `module.exports.ready = true` asynchronously a tick later. `cfg.ready` logs `undefined`. What property of `require` explains this?
options: `require` returns a snapshot of `module.exports` as it stands the instant the call resolves
`require` deep-clones the exported object, so later mutations on the original never propagate across
`require` always returns a Promise, so reading `.ready` synchronously observes the unresolved value
`require` re-runs the module's top-level code on every access, resetting `ready` back to undefined
variants.rationale: `require` executes the target module synchronously to completion and hands back whatever `module.exports` references at that moment. If `ready` is assigned later on a subsequent tick, it wasn't there when `require` returned, so the caller's reference reflects the earlier state. (Because objects are shared by reference, a later mutation would show up if you read the same object again later — but the synchronous read at load time sees the pre-assignment snapshot.)
optionExplanations: Correct — `require` returns `module.exports` as it stands when the call completes; a later async assignment isn't visible to the synchronous read.
`require` shares the exports object by reference; it does not clone, deep or otherwise.
`require` is synchronous and returns the exports object directly, never a Promise — that's ESM `import()`.
Module top-level code runs once and is cached; `require` does not re-execute it per access.
variants.interviewTip: Contrast the two binding models: CommonJS gives you the exports object's value at require time; ESM gives live bindings that track the exporter. That distinction is the crux of most CJS-vs-ESM interview questions.

variants.question: Your project is `"type": "module"`, but you depend on an old library that ships only CommonJS. You need one of its named exports. What's the reliable way to consume it?
options: You cannot use CommonJS from ESM at all; the library has to be rewritten to native ESM first
Import the whole module's default export, then read the named export off that default object
Add `"type": "commonjs"` back so `require` works, which also converts your own files silently
Call `require()` directly inside the ESM file, since Node exposes it globally within every module
variants.rationale: When ESM imports a CommonJS module, Node exposes the module's `module.exports` as the default export. Node's cjs-named-export detection often surfaces named imports too, but the always-reliable path is `import pkg from 'old-lib'` and then `pkg.thing` — because the CommonJS `exports` object becomes precisely that default. This lets a modern ESM codebase keep using legacy CJS dependencies without rewriting them.
optionExplanations: ESM can import CommonJS fine — that direction of interop is supported; it's `require`-ing true ESM that's the hard direction.
Correct — a CommonJS module's `module.exports` arrives as the ESM default import, so read named members off that default object.
Flipping your package back to CommonJS reinterprets all your own `.js` files, breaking your ESM syntax — far too blunt a fix.
`require` is not defined in ESM scope; you'd have to build one via `createRequire(import.meta.url)`, not call a global.
variants.interviewTip: Know both interop directions: ESM importing CJS works (exports → default); CJS `require`-ing real ESM does not, historically needing dynamic `import()`. If you must `require` from ESM, `module.createRequire(import.meta.url)` is the escape hatch.

variants.question: A module needs to `await` a config fetch before exporting a fully-built client. In ESM this is a few lines at module scope; the same thing is awkward in CommonJS. Which ESM capability makes the difference?
options: CommonJS forbids `async` functions entirely, so the config fetch cannot even be expressed there
ESM `import` statements run faster, so the fetch completes before the module body needs it
Top-level `await`: ESM is async-linked, so you can `await` at module scope without an async wrapper
ESM auto-caches network responses, letting the config resolve synchronously on the very first import
variants.rationale: Because ESM is evaluated asynchronously as part of its link phase, it supports top-level `await` — you can pause a module's evaluation on a promise right at module scope, and importers wait for it to finish before their own code runs. CommonJS loads synchronously, so it has no such pause point; you'd have to export a promise or an async init function and make every consumer await it.
optionExplanations: CommonJS supports `async` functions fine; what it lacks is a way to `await` at the top level of the module itself.
Import speed is irrelevant — the issue is being able to suspend module evaluation on a promise, which timing tricks can't provide.
Correct — ESM's async evaluation enables top-level `await`, letting the module pause on the fetch before it finishes exporting.
ESM does no automatic response caching, and a network fetch is inherently asynchronous — it can't resolve synchronously.
variants.interviewTip: Top-level await is the clean ESM answer to 'async work before exports.' Mention the ripple effect: importers of a top-level-awaiting module also wait on it, so use it deliberately — it can serialize your startup.

sections.heading: Authentication: sessions vs JWT
paragraphs: Session-based auth keeps the source of truth on the server: after login the server creates a session record (in memory, Redis, or a database) and sends the client an opaque session id in a cookie. Every request carries the cookie, the server looks up the session, and you can revoke access instantly by deleting the record. The cost is that lookup and shared session storage across every server instance.

JWT (JSON Web Token) auth is stateless: the server signs a token containing the claims (user id, roles, expiry) and hands it to the client, which sends it back on each request. The server verifies the signature and trusts the payload without any lookup — great for horizontal scaling because any instance can validate a token alone. The catch is revocation: a signed token is valid until it expires, so you can't cleanly 'log someone out' server-side without extra machinery (a short expiry plus refresh tokens, or a denylist that reintroduces the state you were avoiding).

Two rules that trip people up. First, JWTs are signed, not encrypted — anyone can base64-decode and read the payload, so never put secrets in it. Second, cookies carrying either credential need protection: `HttpOnly` (blocks JavaScript/XSS theft), `Secure` (HTTPS only), and `SameSite` (mitigates CSRF). Storing a token in `localStorage` forfeits `HttpOnly` and exposes it to any XSS on the page.
sections.summary: Sessions keep state server-side so you can revoke instantly but must share session storage; JWTs are stateless and scale easily but are hard to revoke before expiry — and a JWT is signed, not encrypted, so it's readable by anyone.

variants.question: A team stores user roles inside a JWT and puts the user's plaintext email and an internal flag in the payload too, reasoning 'it's signed, so it's safe.' What's the security flaw?
options: Signing uses a weak default algorithm, so an attacker can trivially forge a token with any roles
A JWT payload is only base64-encoded, not encrypted — anyone holding the token can read every claim
The token will exceed the cookie size limit once the roles are added, so the browser silently drops it
Roles belong in the header, not the payload, so the server will ignore them during verification
variants.rationale: A JWT's signature guarantees integrity — the payload can't be tampered with undetected — but it provides no confidentiality. The payload is just base64url-encoded JSON, trivially decoded by anyone who intercepts or holds the token. Putting a plaintext email or an internal flag there leaks it to the client and anyone in between; secrets and sensitive PII must never live in a JWT.
optionExplanations: The default-algorithm/forgery concern is a different issue; here the payload is signed correctly — the flaw is that signing isn't encryption.
Correct — signing gives integrity, not confidentiality; the base64url payload is readable by anyone with the token.
Cookie size limits aren't the security problem, and roles alone rarely approach the ~4KB limit anyway.
Claims in the payload are exactly where roles belong; the header carries algorithm metadata, and nothing gets ignored on verify.
variants.interviewTip: State it flatly: 'signed, not encrypted.' Then the corollary — never store secrets or sensitive PII in a JWT. If confidentiality is required, you need JWE (encryption) or keep the data server-side behind an opaque token.

variants.question: Security asks you to immediately log out a compromised account across all its devices. Your auth is pure stateless JWT with a 24-hour expiry. Why is instant revocation hard here?
options: The signing key is shared, so revoking one token would invalidate every other user's token as well
Deleting the user's server session ends it, but the browser keeps replaying the cached token anyway
A signed JWT stays valid until it expires; with no server lookup there's nothing to delete to revoke it
JWT logout requires the client itself to voluntarily discard the token, which a compromised device won't do
variants.rationale: Stateless JWT means the server verifies a token's signature and expiry without consulting any store — that's the scaling benefit. But it's also why revocation is hard: there's no server-side record to delete, so a valid, unexpired token keeps working until its 24-hour clock runs out. Practical fixes reintroduce some state: short access-token lifetimes plus revocable refresh tokens, or a token denylist checked on each request.
optionExplanations: Revocation doesn't touch the signing key; rotating that key would indeed invalidate everyone, which is why it's not the revocation mechanism.
Pure stateless JWT has no server session to delete — that's precisely the point; the token itself carries the authority.
Correct — with no server-side record behind the token, there's nothing to remove, so it stays valid until expiry.
Revocation can't depend on a compromised device cooperating; the server needs a mechanism that doesn't trust the client.
variants.interviewTip: The revocation trade-off is the classic sessions-vs-JWT question. Best answer: short-lived access tokens plus a refresh token you can revoke server-side — you keep most of JWT's statelessness while regaining a revocation point.

variants.question: A frontend stores its JWT in `localStorage` and attaches it via an `Authorization` header. A reviewer flags this as riskier than an `HttpOnly` cookie. What's the concrete threat?
options: Any XSS on the page can read `localStorage` and exfiltrate the token, which `HttpOnly` would block
`localStorage` is cleared when the tab closes, so users are logged out and must re-authenticate constantly
Browsers never send `Authorization` headers cross-origin, so the token fails on any third-party API call
`localStorage` values are shared across every origin, leaking the token to unrelated sites the user visits
variants.rationale: `localStorage` is fully readable by any JavaScript running on the page, so a single XSS vulnerability lets an attacker script grab the token and send it anywhere. An `HttpOnly` cookie is invisible to JavaScript, so the same XSS can't read the credential (the browser still attaches it to requests). Cookies bring their own concern — CSRF — which `SameSite` and CSRF tokens address, but they close the XSS-token-theft door that `localStorage` leaves open.
optionExplanations: Correct — `localStorage` is script-readable, so any XSS can steal the token; `HttpOnly` hides the credential from JavaScript entirely.
`localStorage` persists across sessions and tab closes (that's `sessionStorage`), so this isn't why it's risky.
`Authorization` headers work cross-origin fine (subject to CORS); header transport isn't the issue here.
`localStorage` is strictly per-origin and never shared across origins — the isolation model isn't the flaw.
variants.interviewTip: The crisp framing: `localStorage` token → exposed to XSS; `HttpOnly` cookie → exposed to CSRF (mitigated by `SameSite`). Name the threat each choice trades for the other, rather than declaring one universally 'secure.'

variants.question: An app runs behind a load balancer across five Node instances. Users report being randomly logged out. Auth uses in-memory server sessions. What's the root cause?
options: The JWT expiry is set too low, so tokens lapse between requests and force frequent re-logins
Each instance holds its own in-memory sessions, so requests routed to another instance find none
The load balancer strips the session cookie on forwarding, so the id never reaches the app tier
Sessions expire on every deploy, and the five instances are simply restarting on a staggered schedule
variants.rationale: In-memory sessions live in a single process's heap. Behind a load balancer, a user's requests fan out across all five instances, and only the instance that handled login knows about that session — the other four have no record and treat the user as unauthenticated. The fix is shared session storage (Redis, a database) so any instance can resolve any session, or sticky sessions as a weaker workaround.
optionExplanations: The scenario uses server sessions, not JWTs, so token expiry isn't the mechanism; the randomness points to instance routing.
Correct — per-process in-memory sessions aren't shared, so requests hitting a different instance find no session and appear logged out.
A stripped cookie would log everyone out consistently, not randomly; the intermittent pattern is the load-balancer fan-out tell.
Staggered restarts would cause bursts tied to deploys, not the continuous random logouts users describe.
variants.interviewTip: 'Random logouts behind a load balancer' is a scaling tell: session state stuck in one process's memory. Lead with 'externalize session storage (Redis)' — it's the same statelessness lesson JWTs solve differently.

sections.heading: Input validation and security
paragraphs: The first law of server security is: never trust input. Every value from a client — body, query string, headers, path params — is attacker-controlled until you've validated it against an explicit schema (a library like Zod or Joi). Validate at the boundary, reject early with a `400`/`422`, and let the rest of your code assume clean, typed data. Blocklists ('strip these bad characters') lose; allowlists ('accept only this exact shape') win.

Injection happens when untrusted input is concatenated into an interpreter's syntax — SQL, a shell command, a NoSQL query, HTML. The universal defense is separation of code and data: parameterized queries / prepared statements for SQL (the driver sends the query and the values apart, so input can never become syntax), argument arrays instead of shell strings for subprocesses, and context-aware output encoding for HTML to stop XSS. String-building your queries with user input is the vulnerability, not the escaping you bolt on afterward.

Beyond correctness, protect availability and headers. Rate limiting caps how often a client can hit you, blunting brute-force and abuse; a body-size limit stops a giant payload from exhausting memory. Security headers via `helmet` (CSP, HSTS, `X-Content-Type-Options`) harden the browser side, and secrets belong in environment/secret stores, never in the request/response or the codebase.
sections.summary: Validate every input against an allowlist schema at the boundary, defeat injection by keeping code and data separate (parameterized queries, argument arrays, output encoding), and protect availability with rate limits and body-size caps.

variants.question: A login query is built as `"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"`. What's the correct fix for the injection risk, and why does it actually work?
options: Escape quotes in `email` with a regex before building the string, which neutralizes injection attempts
Validate that `email` merely contains an `@` sign, which is enough to block SQL injection payloads entirely
Use a parameterized query so the driver sends SQL and values apart and input can't become syntax
Wrap the query in a transaction so a malicious statement rolls back before it can affect any table row
variants.rationale: The vulnerability is that user input is concatenated into the SQL text, so a crafted value can alter the query's structure. Parameterized queries (prepared statements) send the query template and the parameter values over separate channels; the value is bound as data and never parsed as SQL, so no input — however crafted — can change the statement's meaning. That structural separation, not ad-hoc escaping, is what closes the hole.
optionExplanations: Hand-rolled escaping is fragile — encodings, edge cases, and driver quirks slip through; separating code from data is the robust fix.
Checking for an `@` is input validation, not injection defense; a value like `a@b' OR '1'='1` passes and still injects.
Correct — parameterization binds input as data on a separate channel, so it can never be interpreted as SQL syntax.
A transaction controls atomicity, not parsing — an injected statement executes within it and can still read or damage data.
variants.interviewTip: The one sentence that nails it: 'parameterized queries separate code from data, so input is never parsed as SQL.' Add that escaping is the fragile fallback and validation is defense-in-depth, not the primary control.

variants.question: A public API endpoint accepts sign-up attempts with no throttling. Attackers run credential-stuffing and enumeration against it around the clock. Which control most directly addresses this?
options: Add a strict allowlist schema so malformed sign-up bodies are rejected with a `400` before processing
Rate limiting per client/IP, so a single source can't hammer the endpoint with unlimited attempts
Return a generic `500` on every failed attempt so attackers can't distinguish valid from invalid input
Move the endpoint to HTTPS so the credentials in each attempt are encrypted while in transit to you
variants.rationale: Credential stuffing and enumeration are volume attacks: their power comes from making an enormous number of attempts cheaply. Rate limiting directly caps that volume per client/IP (with account-level limits and CAPTCHAs as complements), turning an unlimited automated attack into a slow, bounded one. Schema validation, generic errors, and HTTPS are all good hygiene but none of them bounds attempt frequency.
optionExplanations: Schema validation rejects malformed bodies but does nothing about a flood of well-formed guesses — the attacker sends valid-shaped payloads.
Correct — rate limiting bounds attempts per source, directly defeating the high-volume nature of stuffing and enumeration.
Uniform error responses reduce information leakage but still let the attacker try unlimited times; they don't slow the flood.
HTTPS protects data in transit; it does nothing to limit how many attempts an attacker can make against the endpoint.
variants.interviewTip: Match the control to the attack's mechanism: volume attacks want rate limiting/CAPTCHA/lockouts; injection wants parameterization; leakage wants uniform errors. Interviewers reward picking the control that attacks the attack's actual leverage.

variants.question: A service runs `exec('convert ' + userFilename + ' out.png')` to process uploads. A filename like `x.jpg; rm -rf /` is catastrophic. What's the root cause and the right fix?
options: Untrusted input is parsed by a shell; use `execFile`/`spawn` with an argument array so it stays data
The `convert` binary is outdated; upgrading ImageMagick to the latest release closes the injection path
The filename wasn't URL-decoded first, so decoding it before the call removes the dangerous shell tokens
`exec` runs as root; dropping the process to an unprivileged user fully prevents the command from injecting
variants.rationale: `exec` runs its argument through a shell, so shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `` ` ``, `$()`) in user input are interpreted as command syntax — the same code-vs-data confusion as SQL injection. `execFile`/`spawn` with an argument array (`execFile('convert', [userFilename, 'out.png'])`) bypasses the shell entirely: the filename is passed as a single argument and can never be parsed as commands, regardless of what characters it contains.
optionExplanations: Correct — the shell parsing is the hole; passing arguments as an array via `execFile`/`spawn` keeps user input as data, not command syntax.
The vulnerability is in how you invoke the shell, not in `convert`'s version; upgrading the tool leaves the injection wide open.
URL-decoding doesn't remove `;` or `$()`; if anything it can reveal more metacharacters — decoding is unrelated to the shell parse.
Least privilege limits blast radius but doesn't stop injection; the attacker still runs arbitrary commands as that unprivileged user.
variants.interviewTip: Command injection is SQL injection's cousin — same code/data confusion, different interpreter. 'Avoid the shell: `spawn`/`execFile` with an args array' is the reflex answer; mention least privilege as defense-in-depth, not the primary fix.

variants.question: A team validates request bodies carefully but leaves query and path parameters unvalidated, assuming those are 'less dangerous.' Why is that assumption wrong?
options: Query strings are always URL-encoded by browsers, so they arrive pre-sanitized and can't carry any payloads
All request parameters are client-controlled and equally attacker-supplied, so each must be validated
Path parameters are validated automatically by the router's pattern, making explicit checks fully redundant
Only `POST` bodies can reach the database layer, so `GET` parameters can't participate in any injection
variants.rationale: Every part of a request the client can set — body, query string, path params, headers, cookies — is attacker-controlled. A malicious value in `GET /items/:id` or `?sort=` reaches your query builder, file paths, or shell just as easily as a body field, so it can drive SQL injection, path traversal, or command injection all the same. Validation must cover the entire request surface, not just the JSON body.
optionExplanations: URL-encoding is a transport format, not sanitization; the server decodes it back to the raw malicious value before your code sees it.
Correct — body, query, path, headers, and cookies are all client-supplied; every one is an untrusted input that needs validation.
A router pattern might match a shape (e.g. digits) but usually doesn't enforce full validity, and many params aren't constrained at all.
`GET` parameters flow into queries, file paths, and commands constantly; the HTTP method has no bearing on injectability.
variants.interviewTip: Say 'the entire request is the attack surface' — body, query, path, headers, cookies. Candidates who only think of the JSON body miss path traversal via a path param and injection via a query string; naming all the sources signals a threat-model mindset.

sections.heading: Config and the 12-factor app
paragraphs: The 12-factor principle for config is: store anything that varies between deploys — database URLs, API keys, feature flags, ports — in the environment, not in the code. The same built artifact should run in dev, staging, and prod with only its environment differing. Hardcoding a connection string, or committing a `.env` file with real secrets, couples your build to one environment and leaks credentials into version control (and everyone's laptop).

Read config once at startup, validate it, and fail fast. A process that boots with a missing or malformed `DATABASE_URL` should crash immediately with a clear message — not limp along and throw a cryptic error on the first request an hour later. Centralize this: parse `process.env` into a typed, validated config object at boot, and let the rest of the app import that object instead of reaching into `process.env` scattered everywhere.

Keep dev/prod parity and treat backing services as attached resources. Config is what lets you swap a local Postgres for a managed one by changing a URL, with no code change. Secrets in real deployments come from a secret manager or the orchestrator's injected environment, `.env` files are a local convenience only (and belong in `.gitignore`), and you never log the resolved secret values.
sections.summary: Put anything that varies between deploys in the environment, not the code; validate config once at startup and fail fast if it's wrong; and keep secrets out of version control and out of your logs.

variants.question: A service hardcodes its production database URL in `db.js`. Following 12-factor config, why is that wrong and what should replace it?
options: It slows startup because the file must be parsed each boot; inline the URL as a constant to speed it up
Config that varies per deploy belongs in the environment, so read the URL from `process.env` instead
Hardcoding is fine for the URL as long as the password portion is separately encrypted within the file
The URL should live in a JSON file committed beside the code so every environment shares one source
variants.rationale: A hardcoded production URL couples the single build artifact to one environment: you can't run the same code in staging without editing and rebuilding, and any credentials in that URL are now committed to version control. 12-factor says config that differs between deploys lives in the environment, so the value comes from `process.env` (validated at startup) and the identical artifact runs anywhere by changing only its environment.
optionExplanations: Parsing cost is negligible and irrelevant; the real problem is environment coupling and committed credentials, which inlining makes worse.
Correct — per-deploy config belongs in the environment; read the URL from `process.env` so one artifact runs in any environment.
Encrypting a substring still commits environment-specific config into the code and complicates rotation — the value shouldn't be in the file at all.
A committed shared JSON file can't differ per environment and still checks secrets into version control — the same coupling problem.
variants.interviewTip: The phrase to use: 'one build artifact, config from the environment.' Then the corollary — the same image runs in every environment by changing only its env vars, which is what makes promotion (dev→staging→prod) clean.

variants.question: An app reads `process.env.STRIPE_KEY` lazily the first time a payment is made. When the variable is unset in a new environment, the failure surfaces as a confusing error during a customer's checkout. What practice would have prevented this?
options: Retry the payment automatically a few times, since the key often loads in on a later attempt anyway
Default the key to an empty string at read time so the checkout code path never throws on it
Validate all required config at startup and fail fast, so a missing key crashes the boot immediately
Catch the error at the payment call site and show the customer a friendlier, more generic failure message
variants.rationale: Reading and validating config lazily means a missing value stays invisible until the exact code path that needs it runs — here, mid-checkout for a real customer. Validating all required config at boot and refusing to start on anything missing or malformed converts a late, user-facing failure into an immediate, obvious deploy-time crash with a clear message. Fail fast at startup is the 12-factor discipline that surfaces misconfiguration before traffic ever arrives.
optionExplanations: An unset environment variable won't materialize on retry; retrying just repeats the same guaranteed failure against the customer.
Defaulting to an empty string hides the misconfiguration and pushes a broken (unauthenticated) call downstream — worse than crashing.
Correct — validate required config at startup and fail fast, so a missing key stops the deploy instead of a customer's checkout.
A friendlier message treats the symptom; the root issue is that the deploy started at all with required config missing.
variants.interviewTip: 'Fail fast at startup' is the config discipline to name. Parse and validate `process.env` into a typed config object at boot; a bad config should break the deploy, never a live request — errors should surface far from the customer.

variants.question: A developer commits a `.env` file containing the real production API keys so teammates 'have what they need.' Why is this a serious mistake?
options: `.env` files are ignored by Node at runtime, so the committed keys wouldn't actually load into the process
The file format is non-portable across operating systems, so teammates on other platforms can't read it
Secrets now live in version-control history permanently and leak to everyone with repo access; git-ignore it
Environment files must be named `.env.production` exactly, so this one simply wouldn't be picked up in prod anyway
variants.rationale: Committing real secrets writes them into git history, where they persist across every clone and branch even if you later delete the file — anyone with repo access (now or in the future) can recover them, so the keys must be rotated. `.env` belongs in `.gitignore`; secrets come from a secret manager or injected environment in real deployments, and the committed file should hold only non-sensitive defaults or a `.env.example` template.
optionExplanations: `.env` files are loaded (via a loader like dotenv or the platform), so the keys very much do reach the process — that's not the issue.
The format is plain `KEY=value` and portable enough; portability isn't the problem, credential exposure is.
Correct — committing secrets embeds them in git history for anyone with repo access; git-ignore `.env` and rotate the exposed keys.
Any filename can hold secrets, and the naming convention is loader-specific; the danger is committing real credentials at all.
variants.interviewTip: Two beats: (1) secrets in git history persist even after deletion, so you must rotate them; (2) `.env` is a local convenience — git-ignore it and use a secret manager or injected env in real deploys. Mentioning rotation shows you've handled a real leak.

variants.question: The same Docker image is promoted dev → staging → prod, each pointing at a different database purely via an injected `DATABASE_URL`. Which 12-factor idea does this most directly demonstrate?
options: Backing services are attached resources, swappable by config with no change to the built artifact
Logs should be treated as event streams written to stdout rather than to managed local files
The build, release, and run stages must be kept strictly separate from one another in the pipeline
Processes should be stateless so any request can be handled by any instance behind the balancer
variants.rationale: Treating the database as an attached resource means the app reaches it only through a config value (`DATABASE_URL`), so pointing at a different database — local, staging, managed prod — is purely an environment change. The identical image runs everywhere; nothing in the code names a specific database. That swap-by-config behavior is exactly the 'backing services as attached resources' factor in action.
optionExplanations: Correct — the database is an attached resource reached via config, so swapping it per environment needs no change to the image.
Log streaming to stdout is a real 12-factor point, but nothing here concerns logging — the scenario is about swapping databases.
Build/release/run separation is a different factor; the artifact promotion touches it, but the database-by-URL swap illustrates attached resources.
Statelessness matters for scaling, but this scenario is specifically about changing which backing service the app attaches to.
variants.interviewTip: 'Backing services as attached resources' means your app never hardcodes which database/queue/cache it uses — only a URL. The payoff to state: one immutable image promoted across environments, differing only by injected config. That's the whole point of build-once-deploy-anywhere.
